solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Court ban miss neglected, being opposed to inquiry

indicators.note: something neglected falls into disorder, so these letters lose their tidy arrangement

parts.note: the fodder, twelve letters

explanation.surface: A court ruling that blocks a girl is ignored by someone who resists investigation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a young woman or a failure, but it only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Obscurantism is the policy of resisting enlightenment and keeping knowledge from people, i.e. hostility to inquiry.

clue.text: Take pewter's half swirling in traditional strong drink — one serves one's own ale

indicators.note: the earlier pieces go inside the drink word that follows
swirling stirs things round, so the letters of that half are jumbled

parts.note: the first half of pewter is PEW, here jumbled
bub is an old word for strong drink, especially beer
R is the recipe abbreviation, from Latin recipe, take

explanation.surface: Someone tips back half a pewter tankard of old-fashioned strong ale.
explanation.walkthrough: BUB wraps round R plus the scrambled half of pewter to give BREWPUB. 'Take' reads as a plain verb, but it is the prescription R.
explanation.definitionFit: A brewpub is a pub that brews its own beer on the premises and sells it to customers.

clue.text: Help? Bit of damp's entered that material for new-laid pitch?

indicators.note: to have entered something is to be inside it, so this letter sits within the call for help

parts.note: SOS is the distress signal, a call for help

indicators.note: a bit of a word is just a small piece of it, here its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of damp

explanation.surface: A groundsman asks whether damp has got into the turf for a freshly laid pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Sods are cut slabs of turf, laid to make a new grass playing surface.

clue.text: Undersize coley racket — that's something to chew on

parts.note: cud is what cattle chew over
a din is a loud noise, a racket

explanation.surface: A fiddle involving small fish gives someone food for thought.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is read in reverse clue order: the chewing part comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuddin is the Scots word for a young coalfish; coley is another name for the coalfish, so an undersize one fits.

clue.text: Fussy earl about to join up, requiring specialised cells

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top
about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the other piece
fussy suggests fiddling and rearranging, so the noble's letters are reordered

parts.note: the letters of earl, rearranged
to unite is to join

explanation.surface: A finicky peer is about to sign up for something that calls for expert cells.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to join up' reads as one phrase about signing up, but 'about' is the container signal and 'up' reverses UNITE inside the jumbled EARL.
explanation.definitionFit: Retinulae are the groups of light-sensitive receptor cells in each unit of an insect's compound eye.

clue.text: Edible seaweed — me too? Certainly not

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Japanese seaweed used to wrap sushi
second meaning: a reply turning down 'me too', i.e. 'neither do I'

explanation.walkthrough: Split as NOR I, the answer is the curt answer to someone asking whether you agree: not me either.
explanation.definitionFit: Nori is the dried seaweed of Japanese cookery; 'nor I' is the negative counterpart of 'me too'.

clue.text: Rattle inside bark? Old-fashioned lure

indicators.note: inside places one piece within the other

parts.note: tan is tree bark used in tanning; it opens around the other piece
to rap is to knock or rattle
the close of the bark word

explanation.surface: A dog owner wonders whether a rattle hidden in a bark is a lure.
explanation.walkthrough: TAN, bark used in tanning, holds RAP.
explanation.definitionFit: Trapan is an archaic spelling of trepan, to ensnare or entrap someone, so it is a dated verb for luring.

clue.text: Name: popular bulrush includes it

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it within, so the plant word wraps the pronoun

parts.note: in means fashionable, popular
a tule is a bulrush of the western US; its first letter comes before the insertion
taken as written
the rest of tule

explanation.surface: A well-liked bulrush is said to contain it, as if naming a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name' is a verb here, not a noun. Tule is the Californian name for a bulrush, and this old word is a variant of entitle.
explanation.definitionFit: To intitule is an old form of entitle: to give a title or name to something.

clue.text: Partly administered quantity of deal say?

indicators.note: partly means only a portion of the next word is used, its letters sitting inside it

parts.note: found inside the word

explanation.surface: A dose has been only partly given, perhaps a share of some deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Deal is not a transaction but softwood timber; 'say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A stere is a cubic metre, a unit for measuring stacked timber such as deal.

clue.text: Did he creep about nefariously. in favour of breaking rule?

indicators.note: breaking smashes the word apart so its letters re-form in a new order

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
the letters of rule, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a man sneaked about wickedly in support of rule-breaking.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a question pointing at the person: 'he' is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A prouler is an early spelling of prowler, someone who creeps about stealthily, often with bad intent.

clue.text: Glandular trouble, sort I'm past after treatment

indicators.note: treatment works on material and changes it, so these letters come out reordered

parts.note: the fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A patient with a gland problem says their kind is over once they've been treated.
explanation.definitionFit: Prostatism is the set of urinary symptoms caused by an enlarged prostate, a gland disorder.

clue.text: Honourable priest in Jersey etc. as alleged in court

parts.note: PR is an abbreviation for priest
taken as written
CI stands for the Channel Islands, of which Jersey is one
pled is a past form of plead, as in a court

explanation.surface: An upright cleric on Jersey is described as he claimed in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' reads as a placing word but is simply the letters IN. Jersey is one of the Channel Islands, off Normandy.
explanation.definitionFit: Principled describes someone acting on firm moral standards, which is what an honourable person does.

clue.text: Somewhat blushful, but up for it, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the word is judged by its sound when spoken, not its spelling

parts.note: up for it means prepared, willing

explanation.surface: Someone blushes a little but is still keen.
explanation.definitionFit: Reddy means reddish, tinged with red, as a slightly blushing face is.

clue.text: Comrade, frequently holding degree

indicators.note: holding means keeping something within, so the abbreviation wraps the other piece

parts.note: fr. is a dictionary abbreviation for frequently; its first letter opens the wrap
rate is a degree of speed or extent
the close of the abbreviation

explanation.surface: A comrade often holds a qualification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Degree' suggests BA or MA, but here it is RATE, wrapped in FR, an abbreviation for frequently.
explanation.definitionFit: Frater is Latin for brother, used for a friar or a fellow member of a brotherhood.

clue.text: Prickly weed I slash back repeatedly

indicators.note: back means the pair of words is read from right to left

parts.note: taken as written
to rip is to slash or tear
the same pair of pieces written a second time

explanation.surface: A gardener hacks away at a thorny weed again and again.
explanation.definitionFit: Piripiri is a New Zealand plant whose burred seed heads stick to clothing and fleeces, so it is a prickly weed.

clue.text: Rising expert more than 50% doubtful — he gives up

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the word is read upwards

parts.note: a oner is an expert, someone outstanding

indicators.note: more than half means the word is cut short, keeping just over half its letters

parts.note: uncertain means doubtful

explanation.surface: A rising specialist, mostly unsure of himself, quits.
explanation.walkthrough: Five of the nine letters of UNCERTAIN are kept, which is more than half.
explanation.definitionFit: A renouncer is a person who formally gives up a claim, right or belief.

clue.text: Scots get used to new food in foreign country

definitions.text: Scots get used to new food
definitions.meaning: first meaning: Scots ..., to wean a child

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures Scots tourists adapting to paella; in fact 'Scots' tags a dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots, to spain is to wean, getting a child used to food other than milk; Spain is also a country abroad.

clue.text: What's artist used to join bits of detail damaged?

definitions.text: What's artist used to join bits of detail damaged?

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged
the clue frames the jumbled letters as what the painter is put into, so he sits inside them

parts.note: the letters of detail, reordered around the painter
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: A restorer asks what glue an artist uses to mend broken pieces of a detail.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: RA set inside a jumble of DETAIL gives a glue for broken pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Araldite is a trademarked epoxy adhesive, the strong glue for sticking broken pieces together.

clue.text: The old man's returned formerly clean plate

parts.note: pa is father, the old man

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: net once meant clean or neat, an obsolete sense

explanation.surface: Dad's come home with a dish once spotless.
explanation.definitionFit: A paten is the shallow plate holding the bread at the Eucharist.

clue.text: Convert. dusky? One whirls noisily

parts.note: to turn something is to convert it
dun is a dull greyish-brown, dusky colour

explanation.surface: A puzzling note about converting something dark.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: the object is swung round on a cord to make its roar.
explanation.definitionFit: A turndun is an Aboriginal bullroarer, a slat of wood whirled on a string to make a humming roar.

clue.text: First off, smashed back hardball

indicators.note: back means the remaining letters are read in reverse
first off means the opening letter is removed

parts.note: smashed is slang for very drunk

explanation.surface: Something got hit back hard in a ball game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smashed' suggests a shot, but it is the slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A knur is a hard knot of wood, and the small hard ball struck in the northern English game of knur and spell.

clue.text: Make fresh changes to section of marmoreal terracing

indicators.note: a section is a cut-out part, so the letters lie within the phrase

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A builder revises part of some marble terraces.
explanation.walkthrough: Marmoreal means made of or like marble.
explanation.definitionFit: To realter is to alter again, making further changes to something.

clue.text: Overseer identifying sounds from the flock

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ..., South African for boss or master
second meaning: the bleats of sheep

explanation.walkthrough: A shepherd seems to be recognising the bleating; really one word is both a boss and the noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Baas is the Afrikaans-derived word for a boss or master; baas are also sheep's bleats.

clue.text: Fine college with a lake round it

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the water word wraps the college

parts.note: taken as written
a mere is a lake; it opens around the other piece
C is the abbreviation for college
the close of mere

explanation.surface: A fine college is set beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like an adjective, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To amerce is to punish with a fine imposed at a court's discretion.

clue.text: Rascal that is after return passage, one sailor should ignore

indicators.note: after places the second piece behind the first

parts.note: lorel is an old word for a rogue or scoundrel

indicators.note: a return passage is a journey back, so the abbreviation is written backwards

parts.note: i.e. stands for id est, that is

explanation.surface: A rogue booked a voyage home that sailors should avoid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passage' seems to belong to the definition, but it belongs to the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lorelei was the Rhine siren whose song lured boatmen onto the rocks, so a sailor should pay her no heed.

clue.text: First of buildings in Lancs town erected as a unit (6, two words)

indicators.note: in puts that letter inside the town's name
in a down entry, erected means stood upright, read from the bottom up

parts.note: Colne is a town in Lancashire; it opens around the other piece

indicators.note: first of means only the opening letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the first letter of buildings
the rest of the town's name

explanation.surface: The first building in a Lancashire town went up all together.
explanation.walkthrough: Colne is a mill town in Lancashire, a county in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: En bloc is French for all together, as one unit.

clue.text: Loose cape that conceals Vestal maiden's outer parts

indicators.note: to conceal is to keep inside, so the letters are tucked in the next words
outer parts says the letters come from where the two words meet at their edges

parts.note: the end of the first word joined to the start of the second

explanation.surface: A loose cape covers the edges of a Vestal Virgin's body.
explanation.definitionFit: A talma is a loose cape or cloak worn in the 19th century, named after the actor Talma.

clue.text: Caliban's pad, say, made of woven ratan

indicators.note: weaving interlaces strands, so these letters are interlaced into a new order

parts.note: the fodder, a variant spelling of rattan

explanation.surface: Caliban's mat, perhaps, made of woven cane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pad' suggests a cushion, but it is slang for a home: Caliban in The Tempest lives in a rocky cave.
explanation.definitionFit: An antar is an old word for a cave, as in Shakespeare's antres; a cave is the dwelling Caliban has.

clue.text: Check start of sailing with tide

indicators.note: start of means only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of sailing
a neap is the tide of least range

explanation.surface: Look at the tide before setting off sailing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check' reads as inspect, but it is the sense of rebuke or nip.
explanation.definitionFit: To sneap is an old word meaning to nip, pinch or rebuke, that is to check someone.

clue.text: Blue or red replacing cross at end of hand on dial

indicators.note: replacing means one piece takes another's place in the word

parts.note: an index is a pointer on a dial
a cross is an X, the last letter here
a red cent is a copper coin, so red stands for cent

explanation.surface: Is a clock hand blue or red?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' and 'red' both look like colours; one is the definition, meaning risqué.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue in the sense of smutty or obscene matches indecent.

clue.text: Part of trawler's catch ending in larder, tinned?

indicators.note: being tinned means being sealed inside a tin, so the letter goes into one

parts.note: tinned food is in a can; the can word opens around the letter

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, the one taken here

parts.note: the last letter of larder
the rest of the can word

explanation.surface: Is the fish a trawler landed at the back of the larder tinned?
explanation.walkthrough: 'tinned' does two jobs: it gives CAN and puts R inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cran is a measure of fresh herrings, about 750 fish, so it is a portion of a boat's haul.

clue.text: Pungent herb to throw out mostly after pulling up

indicators.note: in a down entry, pulling up means the word is read upward
mostly means all but the last letter is kept

parts.note: to evict is to throw out

explanation.surface: A gardener throws out a strong herb, mostly after pulling it up.
explanation.definitionFit: Cive is another name for chives, a pungent onion-flavoured herb.

clue.text: Probable misprint in Shakespeare was exciting, endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: stirred means excited, past tense

explanation.surface: A probable Shakespeare misprint was thrilling, forever.
explanation.definitionFit: Stirre is a form in a Shakespeare text that editors think is probably a printer's error; Chambers records it that way.

clue.text: Chenopod fungus, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: this phrase means the word is matched by how it is spoken

parts.note: blight is a fungal disease of plants

explanation.surface: A goosefoot plant sounds like it has fungal disease.
explanation.definitionFit: Blite is a name for several plants of the goosefoot family, the chenopods.

clue.text: Doctor, see, introduced to grass, struck off?

indicators.note: introduced into something means put within it

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass; it opens around the other pieces
MO is a medical officer
v. stands for Latin vide, see
the close of reed

explanation.surface: A doctor caught with grass asks whether he has been struck off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass' suggests drugs or an informer, but it is the plant REED.
explanation.definitionFit: Struck off means removed from a list or register, as a disgraced doctor is.

clue.text: Fruit and veg, dismal, dodgy eastern corner galleria initially got in

indicators.note: got in means placed inside, so the jumble goes inside the gloomy word
dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so these letters are out of order

parts.note: grey means dull, dismal; it opens around the jumble
E is the abbreviation for eastern
taken as written

indicators.note: initially means only the first letter of the shop word is taken

parts.note: the first letter of galleria
the close of grey

explanation.surface: Produce in a dreary shopping arcade's shady eastern corner.
explanation.walkthrough: A galleria is an arcade of shops.
explanation.definitionFit: Greengrocery is the stock a greengrocer sells, fresh fruit and vegetables.
